slides.title: Title
slides.notes: Open by framing the Introduction as a map rather than a preface. The lecture is about how Euclid's construction practice becomes a modern course in axioms, algebra, models, and invariants. Point out that the source span is short, but it previews nearly every major theme the course will later slow down and prove.

slides.title: Route Map
slides.notes: Use the route map to establish the lecture's governing motion: construction questions expose assumptions, assumptions demand axioms, axioms invite models, and models reveal invariants. The diagram is deliberately directional, because the Introduction is less a list of topics than a chain of mathematical pressures. Ask students to identify which arrows feel like proof needs and which feel like changes of language.

slides.title: Translation Guide
slides.notes: This slide separates book-side language from computational representation. Emphasize that computation is not replacing synthetic geometry; it is making certain assumptions and invariants inspectable. The most important habit is to ask what each representation can check and what it might accidentally hide.

slides.title: Construction Needs Existence
slides.notes: The equilateral construction is small enough to hold in memory, which makes it useful for exposing a hidden premise. Drawing two circles is an operation, but completing the triangle requires an intersection assertion in the plane. Later axiom systems make this kind of existence claim explicit, so this slide is the first bridge from Euclid to foundations.

slides.title: Proof Dependency Graph
slides.notes: Read the dependency graph as a proof-state visual rather than as a decorative flowchart. Data, permitted moves, and inferred objects are different kinds of nodes, and a good proof keeps those roles visible. This is also where students can see why modern foundations care about ordering assumptions before conclusions.

slides.title: Coordinates Enter Deliberately
slides.notes: The Introduction does not treat coordinates as the death of synthetic geometry. Coordinates enter when a geometric problem benefits from arithmetic diagnostics, especially distance, incidence, and intersection tests. The key teaching point is that numerical checks can support a claim without becoming the geometric idea itself.

slides.title: Field-Degree Obstructions
slides.notes: Use constructibility as the first serious example of algebra explaining a geometric limitation. A straightedge-and-compass construction can build a tower of quadratic extensions, so a power-of-two degree is the signature to watch. The table is not a proof of the full theorem, but it trains students to read algebra as a constraint on possible constructions.

slides.title: Area As Invariant
slides.notes: This slide shifts attention from measurement to invariance. The Pythagorean-looking check uses numbers, but the mathematical content is that decomposition preserves area through a comparison of three squares. Stress that the computation is a diagnostic witness for an invariant statement, not a replacement for geometric reasoning.

slides.title: Parallel Postulate Pressure
slides.notes: The parallel postulate matters here because it creates the first major fork in the course's model-building story. In Euclidean geometry, one expects a rigid uniqueness behavior for parallels through a point. The Introduction previews the fact that changing this assumption leads to internally coherent geometries rather than merely bad drawings.

slides.title: Poincare Disk Check
slides.notes: The Poincare disk gives students a visual model where non-Euclidean parallel behavior can be inspected. The important check is the orthogonality condition for boundary intersections, which confirms that the arcs are legitimate disk geodesics. Point to the residual value as a numerical sanity check, not as the reason the model is mathematically valid.

slides.title: Polyhedra Become Data
slides.notes: The polyhedra preview moves geometry toward finite incidence data. Students should notice that vertices, edges, and faces are not merely labels on a picture; they are the structure from which Euler characteristic is computed. This prepares the course to connect visual solids with combinatorics and topology.

slides.title: Euler Dashboard
slides.notes: Keep two levels distinct on this slide. The Platonic table records face counts in the classical solid, while the mesh diagnostics often triangulate faces for computation. The invariant survives both views in these convex examples, which is exactly why Euler characteristic is a durable course theme.

slides.title: Mini Curriculum Audit
slides.notes: The audit table is a rehearsal for how the rest of the course will be read. Each row names a theme, a representation, and the invariant that should fail first if the model is changed carelessly. Encourage students to treat these rows as a checklist for responsible visualization, not as a list of finished theorems.

slides.title: Synthetic And Computational Habits
slides.notes: This slide makes the lecture's methodology explicit. Synthetic reasoning tracks allowed objects and proof obligations, while computational reasoning tracks encodings, residuals, and reproducible checks. The course works best when students use both habits and remain aware of the translation boundary between them.

slides.title: Common Misreadings
slides.notes: Use this as a pause before the recap to clear away tempting simplifications. Modernization does not mean abandoning Euclid, and models do not mean anything goes. The productive view is that Euclid supplies durable questions, while later chapters sharpen the rules under which those questions can be answered.

slides.title: Recap
slides.notes: Close by returning to the Introduction as a route map. The lecture has moved from construction to axioms, from coordinates to field obstructions, from area to invariants, and from parallels to alternative models. The next chapters will slow these previews down into formal systems, examples, and proofs.
